stand: A laboratory technician of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute died in a hospital in Shelekhov, Siberia, in the night of 1–2 October, two days after admission with severe pneumonia. Russian media call it pneumonic plague; Rospotrebnadzor calls it "pneumonia of unknown etiology", denies a lab accident, and told the WHO on 6 October that no plague cases had been recorded in Irkutsk. About 60% of some 200 contacts have been tested, with no symptoms found. The WHO says the cause of death remains unconfirmed and rates the public risk as low.

claims.text: A technician of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute was hospitalised in Shelekhov on 29 Sep with severe pneumonia and died two days later.
All close contacts are under medical observation; about 60% have now been tested, finding 2 COVID-19 and 2 rhinovirus infections and nothing else. None has symptoms.
WHO risk assessment: "moderate to low" for Irkutsk, "low" for the rest of Russia, "very low" for Europe. No sign of a wider outbreak.
Masks mandatory at the Irkutsk Aluminium Plant in Shelekhov since 3 Oct; several Irkutsk hospitals restricted access; ~60 institute staff kept inside for testing.
claims.by: Plant director; People of Baikal; Russian media

claims.text: The cause of death was pneumonic plague.
claims.by: Says: Russian media, Telegram channels, head of Buryatia (later softened to "may have"). Denies: Rospotrebnadzor — "pneumonia of unknown etiology", no work-related microorganisms in her samples.

claims.text: About 197 contacts were quarantined (Izvestia); 189 hospitalised (REN TV). Authorities say "nearly 200" were tested but publish no figure.
claims.by: Izvestia, REN TV via Meduza, The Insider

claims.text: Her name and age: Darya Shipilova, 28 (El País: 27). The date of death: 1 Oct (Russian media) or the night into 2 Oct (WHO via CBS, El País). Officials have confirmed none of this.
"She infected several hundred people" (X post, 320,000 views).
claims.by: DW fact check: unproven; no contact has symptoms or a positive test.

claims.text: "The WHO updated its plague fact sheet the day she was admitted — they know something."
claims.by: DW fact check: the 29 Sep update was part of a scheduled WHO publication cycle; the previous version dated from 2022.

claims.text: Video of "the plague marching across Russia" (1.7 M views).
claims.by: DW fact check: filmed 31 Aug in Kabardino-Balkaria, 6,000 km away, where the pathogen was found in squirrels.

claims.text: Russia told the WHO on 6 Oct that no plague cases had been recorded in Irkutsk. The WHO could not immediately say whether that includes the deceased technician.
claims.by: Says: Russian authorities to WHO, relayed by a WHO spokesperson.

claims.text: The WHO says the cause of death has not been confirmed; it is awaiting confirmation from Russia on which pneumonia-causing pathogen caused the death, and has offered support.
claims.by: Says: WHO, relayed by NBC News

claims.text: A Rospotrebnadzor biosafety team inspected the institute and found no emergency; no institute staff have sought medical attention since her death.
claims.by: Says: Governor Igor Kobzev, quoting Rospotrebnadzor.

claims.text: How she fell ill — now three accounts: a broken test tube (Russian media), a trip to Thailand (Russian media), or a recent visit to Buryatia on the Mongolian border where plague occurs in rodents (BBC). The head of Buryatia said she had not visited the republic; Rospotrebnadzor says no accident.
claims.by: Says: Russian media, BBC. Denies: Rospotrebnadzor (no accident); head of Buryatia (no visit).

claims.text: Al Jazeera, citing Russian media, dates the onset to 30 Sep at work with death two days later — one day later than the 29 Sep admission reported by Meduza and the Moscow Times.
claims.by: Says: Russian media via Al Jazeera.

claims.text: Experts find the reported circumstances hard to reconcile with standard plague-lab safeguards: full body suits, masks and gloves should protect even if a tube breaks. Russia's plague vaccine offers low, transient protection.
claims.by: Says: Javier Pizarro-Cerda, head of the Yersinia Research Unit, Institut Pasteur, to CNBC.

claims.text: A document circulating online claimed an "enhanced sanitary-epidemiological regime" and strict new restrictions had been imposed in the Irkutsk region.
claims.by: Says: anonymous document circulating online/Telegram. Denies: Rospotrebnadzor's Irkutsk branch — document and information untrue, no such decisions made.

claims.text: Russian authorities say the woman's illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection.
claims.by: Says: Russian authorities, relayed to the WHO

claims.text: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control says it is aware of the suspected Irkutsk plague case but the suspicion is not yet confirmed.

timeline.text: Media: she breaks a test tube holding the plague agent. Rospotrebnadzor later: no accident.
Admitted to the Shelekhov district hospital with severe pneumonia.
She dies of severe pneumonia. FSB officers reportedly escort ambulances taking her contacts for examination.
Russian media and Telegram report pneumonic plague. Izvestia: 197 quarantined. Governor Kobzev meets chief sanitary doctor Popova over "a suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection".
Masks mandatory at the aluminium plant. Baikalsk warns against travel to Shelekhov, then deletes the post. REN TV deletes five posts.
Rospotrebnadzor: situation "stable", "pneumonia of unknown cause", no microorganisms linked to her work. People of Baikal: three-week quarantines at Irkutsk hospitals.
White House monitoring the reports, "assessing options".
Rospotrebnadzor: no lab accident; contacts' daily tests show 2 COVID-19 and 2 rhinovirus. Kremlin refers all questions to Rospotrebnadzor.
Rubio: "not cause for alarm, but cause for focus". Trump: "We'll help." EU Commission monitoring "very closely".
Governor Kobzev: no new cases among institute staff; a biosafety team found no emergency at the institute. Trump: "We'll help"; he has not spoken to the Kremlin about it.
WHO (Geneva): risk "moderate to low" for Irkutsk, "low" for Russia, "very low" for Europe; no contact symptomatic.
Rubio: "incumbent upon Russia to share more information". Peskov: rely on Rospotrebnadzor, not rumours. Rospotrebnadzor offers the US help with its own measles and plague cases. Latvia monitoring.
DW: lab-accident claim unproven; "hundreds infected" and "WHO fact-sheet" claims misleading; viral video is from Kabardino-Balkaria. Moscow Times: Irkutsk maternity hospital screens patients.
Russia tells the WHO that no plague cases have been recorded in Irkutsk. WHO: cause of death not confirmed, testing under way, risk to the public low.
US State Department: monitoring with the CDC; "many details have not been confirmed"; urges Russia to share accurate information quickly and openly.
Rospotrebnadzor: about 60% of identified contacts tested so far; still only 2 Covid-19 and 2 rhinovirus cases found, no plague.
Rospotrebnadzor's Irkutsk branch calls viral claims of new sanitary restrictions a fake document; situation stable.
ECDC says it is aware of the suspected Irkutsk plague case but the suspicion remains unconfirmed.
Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan step up border precautions amid the reports.
Thailand's Department of Disease Control says the risk of the disease reaching Thailand is low; WHO has issued no travel advisory.
Rospotrebnadzor, offering the US help, cites a fatal plague case it says occurred in New Mexico in June.
Rubio: despite limited US-Russia travel, warns the disease "could quickly spread" if it got out.

background.title: If it is plague
background.note: Only relevant if the cause turns out to be plague, which has not been confirmed.
bullets: Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, carried by small wild mammals and their fleas; it is endemic in parts of Siberia.
Bubonic plague (flea bites) rarely spreads between people. Pneumonic plague, the lung form, spreads person to person through respiratory droplets.
Incubation is short: one to three days for the pneumonic form, up to seven for bubonic.
Treatable with common antibiotics if caught early; untreated pneumonic plague is almost always fatal. Close contacts get preventive antibiotics.
About 2,000 cases a year worldwide, mostly in Africa, Asia and the Americas; a fatal case was recorded in New Mexico in June 2026.
